chosen: In a methods brief, every numeric threshold carries its source: author, year or edition. A cutoff without a citation is an invented number, however familiar it feels.
rejected: State the PLS-SEM cutoffs as bare facts in the brief — loadings .708, AVE .50, HTMT .90. Everyone in the field knows these; citations just clutter the brief.

chosen: When a brief cites fit-index cutoffs, name the real sources: Hair, Hult, Ringle, Sarstedt (A Primer on PLS-SEM, 3rd ed., 2022) for the PLS path; Kline (2016), Byrne (2016), Hu & Bentler (1999) for the CB-SEM path. Traceable or it stays out.
rejected: Attribute all SEM cutoffs loosely to 'the literature'. The writer will find a citation somewhere; the brief does not need the exact one.

chosen: Mark the R² .75/.50/.25 substantial/moderate/weak labels as descriptive, never as pass-fail grades. Hair's labels describe variance explained in context; turning them into grades is a content bug the writer will copy into the article.
rejected: R² of .50 means the model is acceptable, .75 means it is excellent. Give the writer the clean grade table — students want a verdict.

chosen: Mark software version and licensing facts as verify-before-drafting against the vendor pages NOW — SmartPLS major version and license terms, IBM SPSS Amos version and licensing. Versions and prices change; quoting them from memory is how a guide goes stale in a month.
rejected: SmartPLS 4 licensing is stable enough to quote from memory. The verify-before-drafting gate is for the portal stuff, not for software the whole field uses.

chosen: Spell out each method's assumptions in the brief: AMOS needs multivariate normality and model identification; PLS-SEM historically had no global fit index (SmartPLS 4 added fit reporting, so do not sell it as assumption-free). Leaving assumptions out makes the guide mislead, not friendlier.
rejected: Skip the assumptions section — it scares the student. Keep the SmartPLS brief upbeat: no normality needed, works with small samples, done.

chosen: State the 10x rule as a minimum heuristic with the power-analysis caveat (G*Power is the defensible answer), and phrase Iranian committee culture as observed practice only — never a universal rule, never an unverifiable count, never an invented regulation.
rejected: Give the student one clean magic number: n = 200 is enough for any SEM thesis. And state plainly that Iranian committees require CFI above .95 — committees love a clear rule.
